books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924

stimulus.text: “One of the rights which the freeman has always guarded with most jealous care is that of enjoying the rewards of his own industry. . . . A government which lays taxes on the people not required by urgent public necessity and sound public policy is not a protector of liberty, but an instrument of tyranny.” — President Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain.
stimulus.source_note: Calvin Coolidge, address “Economy in the Interest of All,” June 30, 1924. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain (pre-1930). Text per the American Presidency Project.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Calvin Coolidge, address 'Economy in the Interest of All,' June 30, 1924, public domain
stem: Coolidge's view of government in the passage was most similar to the view held by

options.text: Herbert Hoover, who favored voluntarism and limited federal relief
Franklin Roosevelt, who promised a New Deal of direct relief
options.misconception: Roosevelt broke with Coolidge's view. As governor he said relief was a matter of social duty, and he expanded federal relief.

options.text: Theodore Roosevelt, who used federal power to break up trusts
options.misconception: Theodore Roosevelt used federal power actively, for example against trusts. That is the opposite of Coolidge's limited government.

options.text: Woodrow Wilson, who created the Federal Reserve to manage credit
options.misconception: Wilson built new federal machinery, including the Federal Reserve in 1913. Coolidge wanted government to do less, not to manage credit.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Hoover shared Coolidge's faith in voluntarism and limited government, and he refused direct federal relief even as the Depression deepened.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Roosevelt promised a New Deal and expanded the federal role, the very expansion Coolidge warned against.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Theodore Roosevelt believed in an active federal government, using antitrust suits and regulation, unlike Coolidge.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Wilson created the Federal Reserve to stabilize credit, an expansion of federal power Coolidge would have resisted.
rationales.general:
1. Name Coolidge's view: government should tax little and do little.
2. Ask who shared it. Background from the books: Hoover, his successor, also trusted voluntarism and refused direct relief.
3. Check the others: Roosevelt expanded relief, Theodore Roosevelt used federal power, and Wilson built the Federal Reserve.
4. Hoover held the view most like Coolidge's.
Remember: to compare presidents, match their view of government power, not their party label.
